reference.source: ESC/ERS Guidelines for Pulmonary Hypertension / Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
clinicalPearls: A rare, aggressive cause of pulmonary hypertension in which microscopic tumour emboli seed the small pulmonary vessels and trigger a fibrocellular intimal reaction
Most often associated with adenocarcinomas, particularly gastric and other gastrointestinal, breast, and lung primaries, and may be the presenting feature of an occult malignancy
Presents with rapidly progressive breathlessness, hypoxaemia, and cor pulmonale developing over days to weeks, frequently mistaken for pulmonary embolism or pneumonia
Often accompanied by a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia and raised D-dimer, reflecting widespread microvascular thrombosis
CT pulmonary angiography usually shows no large-vessel thrombus, and perfusion scans may show diffuse peripheral defects rather than segmental mismatches
Diagnosis is frequently made only at autopsy, though wedge or transbronchial cytology and rising tumour markers can support it antemortem
Management is directed at the underlying malignancy, as no targeted pulmonary vascular therapy reverses the process, and prognosis is dismal
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy occurs when malignant cells embolise into the small pulmonary arteries and arterioles and, rather than simply occluding them mechanically, provoke a local activation of coagulation and the release of growth factors. This stimulates a fibrocellular intimal proliferation and in situ thrombosis that progressively narrows and obstructs the microvasculature. The widespread microvascular obstruction rapidly raises pulmonary vascular resistance and imposes an acute pressure load on the right ventricle, producing rapidly progressive pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. The same microvascular thrombotic process shears red cells and consumes platelets, generating the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia that often accompany the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Acute or chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or capillary haemangiomatosis
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or other microangiopathy
Sepsis or pneumonia with acute respiratory deterioration
additionalInvestigations: CT pulmonary angiography, typically without large-vessel thrombus, to help exclude classic embolism
Ventilation-perfusion or perfusion scan, which may show diffuse patchy peripheral defects
Right heart catheterisation to document pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension
Full blood count and blood film for microangiopathic haemolysis and thrombocytopenia
Tumour markers and cross-sectional imaging to identify an underlying malignancy
Pulmonary microvascular cytology from wedged catheter aspiration or lung biopsy where feasible
redFlags: Rapidly progressive breathlessness and hypoxaemia with acute right heart failure
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia suggesting disseminated microvascular disease
Pulmonary hypertension in a patient with known or suspected adenocarcinoma
Deterioration despite treatment for presumed pulmonary embolism or infection
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is extremely poor, with most patients deteriorating over days to weeks, and the diagnosis is frequently confirmed only post mortem. Occasionally, prompt recognition and treatment of the underlying malignancy can slow progression, but survival is generally measured in weeks.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because CT pulmonary angiography shows no large-vessel clot
Attributing rapid deterioration solely to pneumonia or thromboembolism and missing an occult cancer
Overlooking the diagnostic clue of concurrent microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
Expecting targeted pulmonary vasodilators to reverse a fundamentally malignant microvascular process
Delaying a search for the primary tumour that determines any therapeutic option
references: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
management: Identify and treat the underlying malignancy urgently with systemic chemotherapy directed at the primary adenocarcinoma, the only intervention that may slow progression
Provide supportive oxygen and manage acute right heart failure and cor pulmonale
Consider anticoagulation for the widespread in situ microvascular thrombosis
Use pulmonary vasodilator therapy cautiously as a bridging measure where appropriate
Search for and stage the occult primary tumour with cross-sectional imaging, endoscopy and tumour markers
Manage within an oncology-led multidisciplinary team and involve palliative care early given the extremely poor prognosis
Discuss ceilings of care and offer symptom-directed support in view of survival often measured in weeks
